paper.citation: Smiley T, Dallman J, Long R, Kapple M, Aldag L, Mok A, Bernard C, Martin K, Vopat L, Vopat B. Lower extremity return to sport testing: A systematic review. The Knee. 2024;50:115-146.
paper.abstract: This PRISMA systematic review of 114 included studies examined functional and strength tests used to judge return to sport (RTS) after lower-extremity injury. Most studies concerned the knee (85%), particularly anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (82%), and the authors found no standardized RTS clearance criterion.
paper.tldr: Lower-extremity RTS testing evidence is concentrated on the knee and ACL reconstruction, and no standardized clearance criteria exist. The review proposes joint-specific test batteries as a framework for future validation rather than as validated clearance tests.
paper.methods: Systematic searches of PubMed, PubMed Central, Cochrane Library, OVID and Embase followed PRISMA, and ROBINS-I was used for risk of bias. Of 19,189 records, 114 studies (0.6%) met the eligibility criteria, 106 from the database search and 8 from reference lists.
paper.findings: Per the results section, isokinetic dynamometry was used in 44 of 114 studies (39%), and single-leg hop for distance was the most common knee test (48% in Table 3). The authors cite knee benchmarks of 85% limb symmetry for quadriceps, 90% for hamstrings and a hamstring-to-quadriceps ratio above 70%, but state that a uniform pass criterion has not been established; hip and ankle evidence is sparse, with 7 hip and 3 ankle studies.
paper.limitations: No included test was followed through to re-injury after clearance, and most included studies were at moderate to severe risk of bias. Studies often did not control for graft type, concomitant injury, sex or activity level, and the abstract and results section disagree (isokinetic use 73% vs 39%; two vs three ankle studies), so the results-section figures are used here.
paper.practicalImplications: The suggested knee, hip and ankle batteries combine strength (hand-held or isokinetic), hop and landing tests, balance and patient-reported readiness, which can serve as a menu for staff. The review does not supply validated pass thresholds for clearance.
paper.athleteDev: The review concerns rehabilitation testing rather than training outcomes and offers no performance evidence in healthy athletes. Staff may borrow its test menu (strength, hop, landing) as physical-capacity measures, but this application is indirect.
paper.rtp: Directly relevant to return to sport: it catalogs lower-extremity functional tests and their evidence, mainly after ACL reconstruction, and suggests joint-specific batteries. It cannot be used to set validated RTS clearance thresholds, because the review states none exist and no test has been validated against re-injury after clearance; hip and ankle recommendations rest on few studies.
